title: The std::string class
relevance: Interviewers use std::string to check ownership, I/O traps, capacity/SSO, C-interop, and safe building/parsing of text in OAs and SDE rounds.

phases.goal: Establish what std::string is, how it is created and read, and that length differs from capacity.

must_hit.point: std::string (from <string>) is a typedef for std::basic_string<char>; it manages its own storage, grows/shrinks, tracks length, and provides members for searching, editing, and combining text.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names <string>, says it owns storage unlike a fixed char array, and mentions length bookkeeping / member functions.

must_hit.point: cin >> str reads a single word (stops at whitespace); getline(cin, str) reads an entire line including spaces; prefer getline into a std::string over C-style cin.getline(buf, n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts word vs full-line read and states getline is preferred when you already have a std::string.

must_hit.point: size()/length() is characters in use; capacity() is the allocated block size; empty() is true when there are no characters; clear() erases characters so length becomes 0.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates logical length from allocated capacity and names empty/clear correctly.

must_hit.point: Common construction includes empty, count-and-fill like string(5, 'x') → "xxxxx", from a C-string/literal, copy, substring ctor like string(c, 1, 3) → "ell", and initializer_list.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives at least two distinct ctor forms with the file's fill or substring examples.

probes: What is std::string, and how do cin >> and getline differ when reading into one?
How do size/length and capacity differ on a std::string?

hints.1: Think of it as an owning object from <string>, not a bare char array.
hints.2: Contrast whitespace-stopping extraction with whole-line getline, then size vs allocated block.
hints.3: std::string is basic_string<char>; cin >> stops at whitespace, getline keeps spaces; size/length count used chars, capacity is the block, clear sets length to 0.

phases.goal: Explain SSO, contiguous null-terminated storage, resize/reserve semantics, mutation, search, and numeric conversion APIs.

must_hit.point: SSO embeds short strings in the object (no heap); beyond an implementation-defined threshold (commonly around 15 chars for char on 64-bit libstdc++) the object holds a heap pointer; sizeof(std::string) is larger than a pointer (often 24 or 32 on 64-bit libstdc++/libc++); the standard does not mandate SSO but major libraries use it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says short strings avoid heap allocation, explains why sizeof exceeds a pointer, and may cite the ~15 / 24-or-32 figures from the file.

must_hit.point: Since C++11, characters are contiguous and null-terminated: '\0' at data()[size()] is not counted in size(); c_str() and const data() are interchangeable for reading; C++17 adds non-const data(); pointers invalidate after non-const ops that may reallocate.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States contiguous + trailing '\0' not in size, distinguishes c_str/data use, and mentions invalidation on reallocation.

must_hit.point: resize(n) changes logical length (pad/truncate; shrinking length does not free capacity); reserve(n) leaves size unchanged but ensures capacity() >= n; shrink_to_fit is a non-binding request; clear typically keeps capacity; portable drop-buffer idiom is string().swap(s) or move-assign from a temporary empty string.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Clearly separates resize (changes text length) from reserve (growth planning) and notes clear/shrink_to_fit capacity behavior.

must_hit.point: find/rfind and find_first_of/find_last_of return indices; absent search returns string::npos; C++20 starts_with/ends_with and C++23 contains are Boolean prefix/suffix/substring tests.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names npos for not-found and at least one of find family or the modern Boolean queries.

must_hit.point: to_string formats decimal text; sto* (stoi/stol/…) parse with optional idx and base (integers: base in [2, 36] or 0 auto-detect); throw invalid_argument if no conversion and out_of_range if value does not fit; partial prefix parses succeed unless idx is checked against size().
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions throw types and that "42xyz"-style partial success needs idx validation.

probes: Does std::string always allocate on the heap, and why is sizeof(std::string) bigger than a pointer?
What is the difference between reserve and resize?
What does stoi throw, and when does a partial parse still succeed?

hints.1: Short strings and size vs capacity are separate stories from parsing APIs.
hints.2: Cover SSO inline buffer, then resize vs reserve, then contiguous c_str/data, then sto* exceptions/idx.
hints.3: SSO: short text inline, no heap, sizeof often 24/32; reserve plans capacity without changing size, resize changes length; C++11 contiguous + null at data()[size()]; stoi throws invalid_argument/out_of_range and can accept a prefix unless you check idx.

phases.goal: Compare in-place building vs operator+, owning string vs string_view, and sto* vs charconv.

must_hit.point: operator+ builds a new string and chaining creates temporaries (worst fold pattern can be quadratic); +=/append/push_back extend in place and reallocate only when size would exceed capacity; growth is typically geometric so a += loop is amortised linear but still does allocations unless you reserve first.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Prefers +=/append over s = s + piece and explains temporary/allocation cost of +.

must_hit.point: Use std::string when you need ownership, mutation, or a guaranteed null-terminated buffer for C APIs; use std::string_view (C++17) when you only read an existing sequence without copying — string_view does not guarantee null-termination and must not outlive its data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Own vs borrow: string for ownership/C-string need, string_view for non-owning read with lifetime/null caveats.

must_hit.point: For hot/contest parsing, from_chars/to_chars (<charconv>, C++17) work on raw char ranges, are locale-independent, typically faster than sto*/iostreams, and return errc instead of throwing; fall back to stoi/to_string for convenience.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts non-throwing locale-free charconv with throwing sto* convenience.

probes: When building a long string in a loop, why prefer += with reserve over repeated + assignment?
When would you take std::string versus std::string_view as a parameter?
When would you choose from_chars over stoi?

hints.1: Think about whether each step allocates a fresh string or mutates one buffer.
hints.2: Compare new temporaries from + versus in-place append with optional reserve; then ownership vs view; then exceptions vs errc.
hints.3: Prefer reserve then +=/append; string owns/mutates/null-terminates, string_view borrows without guaranteed '\0'; charconv is faster, locale-free, non-throwing for bulk integer parse.

phases.goal: Apply string APIs safely in I/O, C interop, building, and parsing code.

must_hit.point: Do not return s.c_str() from a function when s is a local std::string — the pointer dangles when s is destroyed; return the string by value (or a string_view only while the owner lives).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Identifies dangling c_str from a destroyed local and says return the owning string.

must_hit.point: s.copy(dest, n) copies n characters but does not append '\0' (unlike strcpy); the caller must terminate manually, or prefer c_str()/explicit '\0' for C APIs.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States copy is non-null-terminating and shows manual '\0' or c_str preference.

must_hit.point: When joining many pieces, sum sizes, reserve(total) once, then += each part to avoid realloc churn; prefer push_back/+= for single chars or known pieces.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes one reserve then append pattern for joining.

must_hit.point: Indexed loops should prefer i < s.size() (or iterators/range-for) over stopping at '\0', because embedded '\0' is allowed and counted in size(); C-string-style loops can stop early.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Warns that null-terminated-style iteration can miss chars after an embedded '\0'.

probes: What goes wrong if a function returns the c_str() of a local std::string?
Why is string::copy dangerous compared with c_str() for printing into a char buffer?
How would you efficiently join a vector of strings into one std::string?

hints.1: Lifetime who owns the characters when a pointer escapes a function.
hints.2: Local destruction invalidates c_str; copy omits '\0'; joining should reserve then append.
hints.3: Return std::string by value, not c_str of a local; after copy add '\0' yourself; reserve sum of sizes then +=; iterate with size()/iterators, not only until '\0'.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: + builds a new string and chained + creates temporaries (can be quadratic when repeatedly copying a growing left-hand side); +=/append/push_back mutate in place and only reallocate when capacity is exhausted — geometric growth makes a += loop amortised O(n), and reserve(expected) removes realloc churn.

reserve(n) plans capacity without changing logical text; resize(n) changes length (pad or truncate) and may grow capacity, but shrinking length does not free capacity — confusing them is a common bug when building character by character.

Use string for ownership, mutation, or guaranteed null-terminated C interop; use string_view to read existing text without copying — it is non-owning, not necessarily null-terminated, and must not outlive the viewed data.

sto*/to_string are convenient but sto* throw and accept partial parses unless idx is checked; charconv operates on raw ranges, is locale-independent, typically faster, and reports std::errc without throwing — preferred for contest/hot integer parsing.

gotchas.trap: cin >> str on "hello world" stores only "hello"; mixing cin >> with getline leaves a leftover newline so the next getline can read an empty line.
gotchas.correction: Use getline(cin, str) for whole lines; treat leftover-newline and fast-I/O interaction as a separate I/O topic (s54).

gotchas.trap: Assuming std::string always heap-allocates, or that sizeof(std::string) equals sizeof(char*).
gotchas.correction: With SSO, short strings typically live inline with no heap allocation; the object stores size/capacity (or equivalent) plus an inline buffer, so sizeof is larger than a pointer (often 24 or 32 on 64-bit).

gotchas.trap: Returning s.c_str() when s is a local std::string.
gotchas.correction: The pointer dangles when s is destroyed; return the std::string by value (or a string_view only while the owner lives).
copy does not append '\0'; terminate manually, or prefer c_str() / an explicit null-terminated buffer for C APIs.

gotchas.trap: Building with bad = bad + "x" in a loop, or += without reserve on large builders.
gotchas.correction: Use +=/append/push_back in place; call reserve with a known or upper-bounded final length to avoid repeated reallocations.

gotchas.trap: Treating "no exception from stoi" as "the whole string was a clean number".
gotchas.correction: Partial parses like "42abc" → 42 succeed; check idx against size(). Hard failures throw invalid_argument or out_of_range; prefer charconv when you want non-throwing checks.

gotchas.trap: Passing string_view::data() to a C API expecting a C-string, or letting a string_view outlive its source.
gotchas.correction: string_view is not guaranteed null-terminated and is non-owning; keep the owning string (or other storage) alive, and use std::string/c_str when a C-string is required.

gotchas.trap: Looping while str[i] != '\0' as if the string were only a C string.
gotchas.correction: Prefer i < s.size(), iterators, or range-for; embedded '\0' is allowed and counted in size(), so a C-style stop can end early.
